new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (src StressTyp2) encodes fixed penultimate stress (penultimate stress); Brewer & Brewer state the same placement, penultimate, with no exceptions. The digital copy is the 1971 second printing (facsimile of the 1962 first edition, 'Versión facsimilar'), archive.org item nahuatltetelcingodiccionario;org djvu text.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress always falls on the penultimate syllable; because it is fully predictable, the practical orthography does not mark it.
new_statements.identity_note: Brewer & Brewer 1962 describe the Nahuatl of the village of Tetelcingo, near Cuautla, Morelos (the 'dialecto náhuatl que se habla en la comunidad de Tetelcingo, cercana a Cuautla', Prólogo p. iii), i.e. the tete1251 variety itself (Tuggy's 'Mösiehuali̱'). Pittman 1954 (not opened) describes the same village per its Cambridge extract ('The village of Tetelcingo is six kilometers north of Cuautla, Morelos'). Note that velazquez_patino_2014 in the same folder is about Cuentepec Nahuatl, not Tetelcingo, and was not used.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict penultimate) rests on Tuggy 1979:6, a 140-pp specialist grammatical sketch that we hold in full; the quotation is verbatim at the stated page and section. StressTyp2's independent source (Pittman 1954:13) says the same, and a third primary description downloaded now (Brewer & Brewer 1962:252, 'siempre en la penúltima sílaba') confirms. No later phonology or instrumental study of Tetelcingo stress exists in Glottolog's list or turned up in the (search-budget-limited) web search; the only acoustic prosody paper found for Morelos Nahuatl is on Cuentepec, a different variety. Tuggy's 'very rare exceptions marked with an accent' (e.g. katléhwaw, p. 66 fn.) are lexical and do not disturb a fixed: penultimate syllable coding. tone.quote: There are twenty-three segmental phonemes in this dialect [...] A word is defined for this dialect as any phonological sequence beginning after silence or with the second syllable after a loud stress, and ending with the first syllable following a loud stress, i.e., words are distinguished by penultimate accent. The only exception to this which I have noted is that of the enclitic -ka, kiéni-ka how. [...] Word stress may be marked by either an accent over the stressed vowel or # (space) after the following syllable. [...] The stress-boundary placement between two vowels or two consonants is completely automatic
